title: Remembering Horeb and the Failure at Kadesh
summary: In the fortieth year, on the plains of Moab, Moses begins to explain the law to the new generation. He recalls God's command to leave Horeb and take the land, the appointment of judges to share his burden, and the moment at Kadesh-barnea when their parents refused to go up, grumbling that the LORD hated them. God swore that the evil generation would not see the land, except Caleb and Joshua, and when the people then tried to fight without him, they were routed.
story: Deuteronomy opens where Numbers ended, with Israel camped east of the Jordan across from Jericho, forty years after leaving Egypt. The generation that refused the land has died in the wilderness, and Moses, who will not enter it himself, now addresses their children. Before he restates the law, he retells their history, beginning not with the exodus but with Horeb (the name Deuteronomy usually uses for Mount Sinai), where the covenant was made. The retelling focuses on the great failure recorded in Numbers 13 and 14: the refusal to enter the land at Kadesh. It is placed first because the new generation stands where their parents stood, at the edge of the promise, facing the same choice. Chapter 2 continues the story through the long years of wandering to the first victories east of the Jordan.
historical:
The setting is precise: the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year (verse 3), after the defeat of Sihon, king of the Amorites at Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan (Numbers 21:21-35). Heshbon lay on the plateau east of the northern Dead Sea, and Bashan was the fertile region further north, east of the Sea of Galilee. The place names in verse 1 are harder: several, such as Tophel, Laban, and Dizahab, are otherwise unknown or uncertain, and scholars are unsure whether they mark the site of the speech or recall stages of the wilderness years. Verse 2 notes that the direct route from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea, by way of Mount Seir, took eleven days; the contrast with forty years is deliberate.

The traditional view holds that these are Moses' own words from the end of the wilderness period, which would place them in the late second millennium BC. Many critical scholars date the book's composition much later, to the seventh century BC or after, and read this retelling as addressed to Israel in a later crisis. Either way, the chapter presents itself as the last words of Moses to a people about to enter the land.
cultural:
Moses' appointment of leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens (verse 15) reflects a common way of organizing a large people for both war and judgment, and Exodus 18 tells how Moses first adopted it on the advice of his father-in-law Jethro. In the ancient world, a judge who took bribes or favored the powerful was a familiar evil, and Israel's judges are charged to hear small and great alike and to fear no one, “for judgment belongs to God.” The foreign resident (verse 16) was a non-Israelite living among the people without land or kinship ties, and the command to judge fairly between an Israelite and a foreigner protected someone with no family to defend him.

The Anakim (verse 28) were a people remembered for their great size, associated especially with Hebron (Numbers 13:22, 33). Their reputation terrified Israel's scouts. The picture of fortified cities with walls up to the heavens is exaggeration, but it expresses the dread the scouts felt, and archaeologists have uncovered substantial walls and ramparts at a number of Canaanite cities, which gives that fear a real background.
literary: The chapter is the start of Moses' first address (1:6-4:40), framed by a narrator's introduction (verses 1-5). Moses speaks as a preacher, not a chronicler. He moves between we, you, and I, and repeatedly addresses the new generation as though they had been at Kadesh themselves: “you were unwilling to go up”, even though most of the men who refused are now dead. This technique pulls every later reader into the story. The account differs from Numbers in emphasis. In Numbers 13 God tells Moses to send the scouts; here the people propose it and Moses agrees. Deuteronomy's retelling highlights the people's responsibility and the tender care of God, who carried Israel “as a man carries his son.” The chapter ends heavily, with the people weeping before a God who would not listen and staying at Kadesh a very long time.

outline.t: Introduction: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab
God's command to leave Horeb and take the land
From Horeb to Kadesh; the scouts' report
The people's refusal and Moses' plea
God's oath: the evil generation will not see the land
The failed attack and the long stay at Kadesh

doctrines.note: The heart of Israel's failure was that they “did not trust the LORD your God”, despite everything they had seen. Faith in Deuteronomy is trusting God's word and acting on it, and unbelief is refusing to go where he leads.
God's oath excluded an entire generation from the land. Their late attempt to fight without him also failed, showing that obedience cannot be done on one's own terms after God has spoken.

Moses reminds Israel that God went before them in fire and cloud to find them a place to camp, and carried them as a father carries his son. Even the story of failure is told against the background of God's care.

words.note: Marah, to rebel. The word describes defiant disobedience, especially against a parent or ruler. Moses uses it twice here: “you rebelled against the command of the LORD your God” (verses 26 and 43). The first rebellion was refusing to go; the second was going when God said not to. Both were the same sin in different forms.

Aman, to be firm or trustworthy, and in this form to trust or believe. It is the verb used of Abraham, who believed the LORD (Genesis 15:6). In verse 32 the people did not trust the LORD. The word amen comes from the same root, the response of someone who treats God's word as firm and reliable.

Nasa, to lift, carry, or bear. Moses cannot bear the people's burdens alone (verses 9 and 12), but the LORD carried them in the wilderness “as a man carries his son” (verse 31). The same verb holds together Moses' limits and God's strength.

Shaphat, to judge. In Israel judging meant more than handing down verdicts; it meant setting things right, defending the weak, and ruling justly. The judges are to judge fairly between brothers and foreigners, since judgment ultimately belongs to God.

christ: The New Testament reads the wilderness generation as a warning and a mirror. Hebrews, quoting Psalm 95, asks, “And with whom was God angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?” and concludes that “it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter” (Hebrews 3:17, 19). It then urges believers to enter God's rest by faith. The picture of the LORD carrying Israel “as a man carries his son” anticipates the New Testament's revelation of God as Father, and Jesus, the faithful Son, succeeds where Israel failed, trusting his Father in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11). The contrast between Israel's refusal at the edge of the land and Jesus' obedience is one the Gospels invite readers to notice, especially since his answers to the tempter come from Deuteronomy itself.

hard.q: Why does Moses say God was angry with him because of the people, when Numbers says Moses was excluded for his own sin?
hard.a: In verse 37 Moses says that the LORD was angry with him “on your account” and forbade him to enter the land. Numbers 20:12 says Moses and Aaron were excluded because they did not trust God enough to treat him as holy at the waters of Meribah. Several explanations are offered. Many interpreters see no contradiction: Moses' failure at Meribah happened because of the people's quarreling, so both accounts are true, and Deuteronomy highlights the people's role while Numbers highlights Moses' own act (Deuteronomy 32:51 also names his breaking faith at Meribah). Others suggest that Deuteronomy presents Moses as sharing the fate of the people he led, bearing the consequence of their rebellion with them. Critical scholars often see two different traditions about why Moses did not enter the land, preserved side by side. A similar question arises over the scouts, whom Numbers says God commanded and Deuteronomy says the people proposed; here too, both can be true, with Deuteronomy stressing the people's initiative.

questions: Moses retold the story of Kadesh to people who were children at the time, speaking as if they had been there. How does remembering the failures of an earlier generation help you avoid repeating them?
The people first refused to go when God said go, then went when God said stop. Where do you see the same pattern in your own obedience?
Moses describes God carrying Israel as a man carries his son. What does that image of God mean to you, and how does it shape the way you read the rest of the chapter?
